title: Input Validation and Output Encoding knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which approach best supports reliable work with Input Validation and Output Encoding?
options: Skip input validation because Node.js applications run on a trusted server.
Assume every supported runtime has identical APIs and scheduling behavior.
Store credentials and production secrets directly in the source file.
State whether data is text or bytes, choose the encoding explicitly, and validate decoded length and format.
questions.answer_key: State whether data is text or bytes, choose the encoding explicitly, and validate decoded length and format.
questions.explanation: State whether data is text or bytes, choose the encoding explicitly, and validate decoded length and format. The example and verification steps should make this practice observable.

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under Input Validation and Output Encoding?
questions.explanation: “Validating all untrusted input” is one of the subtopics retained from the supplied Node.js curriculum for this lesson.

questions.prompt: Before relying on a Input Validation and Output Encoding implementation, what verification is most useful?
options: Use the same code regardless of documented version differences.
Verify the documented result in a supported runtime and test one failure or boundary case.
Assume the API behaves as expected without running a check.
Ignore failures so the program continues silently.
questions.answer_key: Verify the documented result in a supported runtime and test one failure or boundary case.
questions.explanation: A small deterministic check plus a failure/boundary case helps distinguish a correct design from a happy-path-only example.
